title: Password managers: a separate secret for every site
body_md:
## When the flower shop is breached

A small online florist loses its customer database, and your password is in it. It is also the password on your email. Nobody has to attack your inbox: whoever gets the list simply tries the same combination there. That is the case for a password manager. It stores and generates your credentials so that every site can have a different password, and its value is containment: when a shop leaks one secret, the damage stays with the shop. A manager can be a reputable browser or platform feature or a separate app. Judge the product by its security and its recovery design, and do not assume one kind is always safe.

### What changes when you sign in

Create a long, unique primary passphrase that you can actually remember. If the vault syncs, protect it with the strongest MFA it supports, and protect every device that can open it. Let the generator make a different password for each account, and save the **verified** address of the site in the same record. Before you change a password, check which account you are in and that the new entry really saved; test the sign-in on a trusted device before you delete the old record. For a work account, follow the storage rules your employer has approved.

Autofill doubles as an alarm. When a saved login fails to appear on the page you are on, the mismatch deserves a look, though it is no verdict. Forms, subdomains, app links and manager settings can stop a fill on a perfectly genuine page, and loose matching settings can fill where they should not. If nothing fills, stop, read the full address and open the service yourself. Never paste a valuable password by hand into a form you do not recognise just to “fix” the problem.

### Plan for the day it fails

A vault puts everything in one place, which is both its point and its risk. Malware on the device, or a shared computer left open, can undo much of its protection, and a weak or reused primary passphrase is dangerous. Learn how recovery works **before** you depend on the product. With some, nobody can open the vault if you lose the secret that decrypts it, like a safe whose maker kept no spare combination; others offer account recovery, with trade-offs of their own. Make an offline recovery plan that suits your product, and name a person you trust if you need one.

Never leave a plaintext CSV export lying in Downloads or in a shared cloud folder. If you are moving to another manager, protect the file, check that the import worked, then delete the temporary copy securely, as your device policy requires.

Start with your primary email and your financial accounts. Replace reused passwords in batches you can manage, then work through the rest. There is no need to change a unique password that has never been exposed just because the calendar says so; change a secret when it is compromised, reused or weak, or when the service demands it. A manager cuts down reuse. It cannot make a fake page safe or heal an infected device.

widget_config.goal: Set up a manager so that each important account has a password of its own and a recovery route you have tested.
widget_config.today_action: Choose one manager you trust and secure its primary account. Then move one high-value login into it with a generated unique password, and check the saved entry before you end the session.
widget_config.scope: General education; product features and employers’ rules differ. The UK NCSC’s criteria for organisations are recast here as questions for an individual. The cases and exercises are invented. Checked 2026-10-20.

blocks.title: A checkout page that does not know you
blocks.situation: A message from an online store sends you to `checkout.support-example.test`. Your saved login for the store never appears, and the page asks for your vault password instead.
blocks.analysis: A strange address and a request for the vault’s primary secret are each reason enough to stop. Open the store from your own bookmark and check the account there. The vault passphrase is never typed into a store checkout.

blocks.title: The university moved its login
blocks.situation: A university has moved sign-in to a single-sign-on subdomain and documents the change. Your password manager does not fill the form, but the university’s own help page links to that subdomain.
blocks.analysis: A missing fill proves nothing by itself. Confirm the change on the university’s own site or with its IT desk, and only then update the address your saved login should match.

blocks.title: Moving one account into the vault
blocks.setup: An invented example: you are moving your account on a neighbourhood marketplace into a password manager on your own laptop.

steps.prompt: The manager offers a random password for the account. What do you save?

choices.text: The generated password, together with the confirmed address of the site.
choices.consequence: The account gets a secret of its own, tied to its real address.
choices.explanation: A unique password rules out reuse, and a correct address helps the manager recognise the site later.

choices.text: Your usual password with one new symbol added.
choices.consequence: The pattern is still reused, or easy to guess.
choices.explanation: A small tweak does not reliably separate this account from your old secrets.

steps.prompt: You have changed the password, but the manager does not seem to have saved the new entry. What now?

choices.text: Sign out everywhere and trust that sync will sort it out.
choices.consequence: You may lock yourself out of the account.
choices.explanation: Check the saved entry and the sync before you end the working session.

choices.text: Open the vault record and test a fresh sign-in while the account session still works.
choices.consequence: You confirm the new secret before you need it.
choices.explanation: A page saying “password changed” does not prove the manager stored that exact value.

steps.prompt: Some weeks later a login form will not autofill. What is the safest response?

choices.text: Paste the password in by hand, since managers often fail.
choices.consequence: A form you do not know may receive your password.
choices.explanation: Typing it in yourself throws away your chance to check where you are.

choices.text: Stop, read the address and reach the service by your own route before touching the matching settings.
choices.consequence: A harmless form change and a fake site stay distinguishable.
choices.explanation: Autofill is a clue, not a final ruling.

steps.prompt: You exported a CSV file to switch to another manager. What closes the migration?

choices.text: Check the import, then delete the unencrypted export from temporary storage as your device policy requires.
choices.consequence: No readable copy of the vault is left lying around.
choices.explanation: An export can hold the whole vault in readable form.

choices.text: Keep the CSV in a shared cloud folder as a handy backup.
choices.consequence: Anyone with access to the folder can read every password.
choices.explanation: Use the manager’s own secure backup or recovery method instead.

blocks.debrief: A manager ends reuse only when the saved address, the generated secret, the protection on the vault and the recovery plan have all been checked. Go back to the step where you let a doubt pass and try it again.

questions.prompt: A site you trust changes its sign-in subdomain and autofill stops. What do you do?

choices.text: Treat the missing fill as proof of phishing.
choices.explanation: Managers can fail to match genuine forms and subdomains.

choices.text: Confirm the subdomain through the service’s own channel before you update the saved match.
choices.explanation: Genuine changes to a sign-in form do happen; establish the address first.

questions.prompt: Why is a plaintext export of the vault so sensitive?

choices.text: It can expose many accounts at once, outside the vault’s usual protection.
choices.explanation: A migration copy should live briefly and under control.

choices.text: It holds only usernames, never passwords.
choices.explanation: A CSV export can include passwords in readable form.

questions.prompt: Which primary passphrase is a good one?

choices.text: The one you already use for email; it is easy to remember.
choices.explanation: Reuse ties your two most important accounts together.

choices.text: A long, unique phrase, protected by the manager’s supported MFA and a recovery plan.
choices.explanation: The vault deserves a secret of its own and an access plan you have tested.
